final.format: 7) Relatable reward: names a habit most practitioners know (bracing, holding the breath, fighting the teacher's hands, or being scared to be touched), then walks through 5 steps to get better at it (speak, exhale, soften, stop, notice). It promises getting better, not never feeling it again.
final.title: Being Adjusted Is a Skill
final.stakes: Stakes: if nothing changes, adjustments stay a fight. You brace and hold your breath, so you feel mostly pressure and miss what the hands came to show you. Most of the help is gone the moment the hands leave. Some people go further and avoid hands, or skip Mysore class, because being touched feels scary and they don't know they can say stop.
final.why_care: Why care: tomorrow morning you will be on the mat again. If you train in Bangkok, a Mysore class can have a few moments of hands-on help, and each one you brace through is mostly lost. If you practise alone at home in China, you may get a teacher's hands only a few times a year at a workshop, so each one counts. Five small steps can make the next adjustment calmer and help you keep more of what it shows you.

slides.text: The teacher's hands come and you brace? Being adjusted is a skill, and half of it is your job.
slides.photo_hint: Clear, calm adjustment of a beginner or an elder (Plato cover rule), e.g. light hands at the hips in a drop back or a forward fold. Empty wall or floor at the top or bottom edge for BRACE. The student's face is calm, not strained.
slides.source: none (teacher's own teaching content; 'half' is a picture, not a number)

slides.text: When the teacher's hands guide you somewhere new, your body tenses to guard itself. Holding your breath and pushing back are the same guard. It is normal.
slides.photo_hint: Deep backbend or drop back, light hands at the hips. The student's face is calm or turned away, working but not strained, so GUARD names the viewer's habit, not this student.

slides.text: Fight the hands and you miss what they came to show you. A tight body mostly feels pressure. A soft body can feel where the hands are guiding it.
slides.photo_hint: Seated twist with one light teacher hand showing the direction. The student is calm, never strained, and the teacher is not pulling hard.

slides.text: Speak before the hands come. Don't wait until it hurts. Tell the teacher about an old injury or a sore knee. Hands help best when they know where not to go.
slides.photo_hint: The teacher kneels or bends close beside the student as if checking or talking, just before or at the start of an adjustment. A forward fold or a seated asana works best.

slides.text: Exhale when the hands come, not after they go. Holding the breath makes the whole body hold. The breath leads. The hands follow.
slides.photo_hint: A forward fold (Paschimottanasana, Prasarita or Uttanasana) with a light flat hand on the back. The student's face and shoulders look soft, as if breathing out.
slides.source: none (teacher's own teaching content; 'the breath leads' is the safety rule from the brief)

slides.text: Soften, and the asana gets steadier, not weaker. The Yoga Sutra says asana is 'firm and pleasant', and comes 'by slight effort'. Keep the firm part. Let the rest go soft.
slides.credit: Yoga Sutra 2.46-47 · tr. Vivekananda, Raja Yoga, 1896
slides.photo_hint: A backbend (Urdhva Dhanurasana) or a supported drop back. The legs are strong while the face, neck and hands look relaxed, and the teacher's hands support rather than push.
slides.source: https://archive.org/download/yogaphilosophyle00viverich/yogaphilosophyle00viverich_djvu.txt (Swami Vivekananda, Yoga Philosophy: Lectures delivered in New York, winter of 1895-6, on Raja Yoga, Longmans, Green, and Co., 1896, pp. 183-184). Re-checked in this step from the downloaded text. Exact words: '46. Posture is that which is firm and pleasant.' and '47. By slight effort and meditating on the unlimited (posture becomes firm and pleasant).' Line 46 is also on https://vivekavani.com/?p=514. The Sanskrit 'sthira sukham asanam' has the word asana, so 'says asana is' is fair. Only 'firm and pleasant' and 'by slight effort' are in quote marks.

slides.text: Saying stop is not rude: it is part of the practice. Scared to be touched at all? Say so. A good teacher asks or checks first, uses light hands and never forces.
slides.photo_hint: The gentlest photo in the set: one or two light hands, the student calm. A standing asana, a simple twist, or the teacher checking in by eye contact. Never a photo where the teacher's body weight is on the student or the student looks in pain.
slides.source: none (the safety rules from the brief: the student can say no, the teacher asks or checks first, light hands, never force)

slides.text: Notice the new place before the hands leave, or the lesson leaves with them. Feel which part moved, and which way. Tomorrow, look for that feeling on your own.
slides.photo_hint: A handstand or a lift-off with the teacher's hands at the hips or thighs showing a clear direction (up, back). Keep text off the space that shows the student lifting from the floor.
slides.source: none (allowed fact: Boonchu's method 'drawing the cortical map', in plain words: the cue says which part and which direction. The method name and the map picture are left off the slide, so there is no study claim.)

slides.text: You can ask for hands, too. Stuck in one asana? Tell the teacher before you start. Asking is not weak. It tells the teacher where to look.
slides.photo_hint: An experienced student in an advanced asana (deep drop back, Kapotasana, handstand) getting light help. Use his wife only if she says OK. Otherwise any clearly experienced student.
slides.source: none (Plato edit 6 Nov: wife/gymnast story kept only in carousel 2)

slides.text: You get better at this, not perfect. Some days you still tense up. It grows class by class: same practice, same time, a teacher who notices when you are gone.
slides.photo_hint: A warm, calm moment: an adjustment at the end of a backbend or a forward fold, the student relaxed or smiling, or a wider view of the Mysore room with the teacher helping one student while others practise.
slides.source: none (allowed fact: AYBKK's promise, 'same practice, same time, a teacher who notices when you are gone')

final.caption:
Do you hold your breath when the teacher's hands come?
An adjustment is when the teacher's hands help you in an asana. Your half of the job: speak, breathe out, soften, say stop if you need, notice.
You can say no at any time. Light hands, never force.
Same practice, same time, a teacher who notices when you are gone.
Comment aybkk and I'll send you the link.
#aybkk #ashtanga #ashtangabangkok #boonchutanti #mysore
final.notes:

The slide still works with 2 sentences.

Confirm it, or it becomes 'A good teacher uses light hands and never forces.'
4. Slides 1-4 and 6-9 are credited as your teaching (AYBKK MYSORE NOTES). Please check that each one is how you teach: the body tenses to guard itself in a new place (1); a tight body mostly feels pressure (2); tell the teacher about old injuries before the hands come (3); exhale when the hands come, the breath leads (4); softening makes the asana steadier (5, your line next to the sutra); notice which part moved and which way, then look for that feeling on your own the next day (7); the skill grows class by class (9).
5. Slide 7: your method name ('drawing the cortical map') and the 'map of your body in your brain' picture are not on the slides now. The reader check said the picture gave no action, so sentence 2 is now the action 'Feel which part moved, and which way.' If you want the map shown, it can go in place of sentence 3 ('Picture a map of your body in your brain.'), or the credit can read 'AYBKK MYSORE NOTES · drawing the cortical map'. 'Function over shape' is not used anywhere.

8. Source re-checked in this step for slide 5 (Vivekananda, Raja Yoga, 1896, aphorisms 2.46-47, pp. 183-184). The exact words match. Only 'firm and pleasant' and 'by slight effort' are in quote marks. No other study, number or quote is used.
Editor's changes (for your information):

- Slide 7: the reader check offered 'Tomorrow, find it again with no hands.' I did not use it, because it could push a student to chase a deep backbend or drop back alone. It now reads 'Tomorrow, look for that feeling on your own.'
- Slide 3 now says 'Speak before the hands come. Don't wait until it hurts.' so it no longer clashes with 'say stop at any time'.

Still open from before:
- Photos: this step wrote the text only. Plato's photo rules apply: the cover shows a beginner or an elder, at most 2 photos of the same student, mix early and late class photos, and no photo where the teacher's weight is on the student or the student looks in pain. Students in the photos must be OK with being posted.
- Keyword test (until 22 Nov): this is a Lane B post (ask: comment aybkk, Instagram only). Please check the A/B mix before it goes out. There is no website, 'come practice' or 'link in bio' on any slide.

issues.problem: Safety wording. 'Speak before the hands come, not after it hurts' can be read as 'do not speak up once it hurts'. That clashes with slide 6 and the caption, which say the student can say stop at any time.
issues.fix: Change sentence 1 to: 'Speak before the hands come. Don't wait until it hurts.' The slide stays at 31 words and 4 sentences, and SPEAK is still in sentence 1.

issues.problem: Photo hint. GUARD ('your body tenses...') goes over a real student who is 'clearly working hard' in a deep backbend. That labels the student in the photo as the one bracing, which breaks two rules: no shaming students, and Plato's rule from 4 Oct, 'never film a student failing as the problem shot'. It also comes close to the 'student looks in pain' photo ban.
issues.fix: Change the hint to: 'Deep backbend or drop back, light hands at the hips. The student's face is calm or turned away, working but not strained, so GUARD names the viewer's habit, not this student.'

issues.problem: Photo hint. FIGHT goes over a two-handed twist adjustment on a real student. The word can read as 'this student fights', and a strong twist adjustment captioned FIGHT invites the 'forceful adjustment' comments that the 4 Oct reel check warned about (it said to show one light hand only).
issues.fix: Change the hint to: 'Seated twist with one light teacher hand showing the direction. The student is calm, never strained, and the teacher is not pulling hard.'

issues.problem: Plain English. 'tenses to guard a place it has never been' is unclear: you cannot guard a place you have never been.
issues.fix: Change it to: 'your body tenses to guard itself in a place it has never been.' The slide goes to 30 words.

issues.problem: The rule is 'true stakes only', and the brief says more than the slides do. 'You feel only pressure' and 'The help is gone the moment the hands leave' are absolute, while slide 2 says 'mostly feels pressure'.
issues.fix: Change to 'so you feel mostly pressure' and 'Most of the help is gone the moment the hands leave.'

issues.problem: 'Every class you pay for has a few moments of hands-on help' is a claim about AYBKK classes. It is not in the allowed facts, and it is not true for a student who has said no to hands.
issues.fix: Change it to: 'a Mysore class can have a few moments of hands-on help, and each one you brace through is mostly lost.'

issues.problem: Note 2 says the safety line is a general rule, not a promise about AYBKK. But the caption, posted by AYBKK in first person, says 'You can say no at any time. Light hands, never force.', which reads as the shala's own promise before Boonchu has said yes to that.
issues.fix: Add one line to note 2: 'The caption line "You can say no at any time. Light hands, never force." already reads as the shala's rule. Confirm it, or it becomes "A good teacher uses light hands and never forces."'

issues.problem: Sentence 1 does not make sense on a literal read: 'tenses to guard a place it has never been'. You guard the place you are in, not a place you have never been. A 10-year-old will trip on it, and it sounds poetic and AI-written. The idea (bracing is the body guarding itself in a new range) is good, but the words hide it.
issues.fix: GUARD: When the teacher's hands take you somewhere new, your body tenses to guard itself. Holding your breath and pushing back are the same guard. It is normal. (27 words)

issues.problem: Sentence 2 is hard to read: "calls asana 'firm and pleasant', found 'by slight effort'". It is not clear what is 'found', and the phrase reads like a footnote. The 35-year-old reader stops here. The quote words are correct (Vivekananda 2.46-47). Only the grammar around them needs to change.
issues.fix: SOFTEN: Soften, and the asana gets steadier, not weaker. The Yoga Sutra says asana is 'firm and pleasant', and comes 'by slight effort'. Keep the firm part. Let the rest go soft. (31 words, same credit. Only 'firm and pleasant' and 'by slight effort' stay in quote marks, and both match the source.)

issues.problem: This is the step where the reader keeps the lesson, but it gives a picture ('a map of your body in your brain') and no action. The reader still does not know what to do in the moment. 'Picture a map... the hands draw on it' is abstract for a 10-year-old and sounds like a hidden science claim. It also repeats the 'before the hands X' pattern from slides 3 and 4, so the how needs to be very concrete here.
issues.fix: NOTICE: Notice the new place before the hands leave, or the lesson leaves with them. Feel which part moved, and which way. Tomorrow, find it again with no hands. (29 words. If Boonchu wants his map method shown, put 'Picture a map of your body in your brain' in place of sentence 3. Keep 'Feel which part moved, and which way' as the action.)

issues.problem: 'An experienced practitioner' is not 10-year-old English. Sentence 3 lands flat: 'asked him for an adjustment' gives no reason to care. Without 'still' or 'for years', the point (even skilled people want hands) gets lost. Her OK is still needed (notes item 1).
issues.fix: SKILLED: Skilled people still ask for hands, now and then. Gymnasts and ballet dancers get a coach's hands too. Boonchu's wife has practised for years, and she still asked him for help. (31 words. 'Still' here means 'even so', not 'every day', so the retold fact stays true. If she says no, cut sentence 3. The slide works with 2 sentences.)

issues.problem: Sentence 3, the AYBKK promise 'a teacher who notices when you are gone', comes after 'you will still tense up' with no link. It reads like a slogan stuck on the end. The same line also closes the caption, so the reader gets it twice.
issues.fix: BETTER: You get better at this, not perfect. Some days you still tense up. It grows class by class: same practice, same time, a teacher who notices when you are gone. (30 words. 'Class by class' links the skill to the habit. Keeps the 'better, not never' promise from the format.)

issues.problem: Mostly works: BRACE is in line 1, the reader asks 'do I do that?', and 'your job' flips the belief that the teacher does all the work. But the main idea, the title 'Being Adjusted Is a Skill', is not on the cover, and 'half your job' alone is a bit vague for a one-second read. Small fix, not a blocker.
issues.fix: BRACE: The teacher's hands come and you brace? Being adjusted is a skill, and half of it is your job. (Credit stays '9 notes · swipe'. It is clear first, with skill as the topic, then clever, with 'your job'. 'Half' is still a picture, not a number.)
